Confusable pairs among the sign shapes and colors, route markers and pavement markings, each tied to one handbook page; hint metadata sits only in trailing lines.

FACT_ID: sec15-R01 | anchor: A01
A stop sign always demands a full stop, while a yield sign demands slowing and yielding, with a stop only when cross traffic requires it. [A01]
Why it matters: group regulatory signs; difficulty high; confusable stop versus yield duty.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec15-R02 | anchor: A01
The octagon belongs to the stop sign alone, while the downward-pointing triangle belongs to the yield sign. [A01]
Why it matters: group sign shapes; difficulty medium.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec15-R03 | anchor: A02
A diamond in black on yellow is an ordinary warning, while a diamond in black on orange warns of a construction or maintenance area. [A02]
Why it matters: group warning colors; difficulty high; confusable yellow versus orange.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec15-R04 | anchor: A02
The yellow pennant on the left marks where a no-passing zone begins, while the rectangular DO NOT PASS sign states the rule itself. [A02]
Why it matters: group no-passing signs; difficulty medium; confusable warning versus regulatory.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec15-R05 | anchor: A02
The round yellow RR sign gives advance warning before the crossing, while the white crossbuck stands at the crossing itself. [A02]
Why it matters: group railroad signs; difficulty medium; confusable advance versus at-crossing.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec15-R06 | anchor: A03
The five-sided pentagon sign warns of a school zone or a school crossing, where drivers should be especially watchful for children [A03].
Why it matters: group sign shapes; difficulty high; confusable pentagon versus octagon.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec15-R07 | anchor: A03
U.S. route markers are shields, interstate markers are red, white and blue shields, and North Carolina route markers are diamonds. [A03]
Why it matters: group route markers; difficulty high; confusable U.S. versus interstate versus state.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec15-R08 | anchor: A03
Odd-numbered highways generally run north to south, whereas even-numbered highways generally run east to west. [A03]
Why it matters: group highway numbers; difficulty medium.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec15-R09 | anchor: A05
Yellow lines separate opposite-direction traffic, while white lines separate traffic moving the same way. [A05]
Why it matters: group line colors; difficulty medium; confusable yellow versus white.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec15-R10 | anchor: A05
A broken yellow line on your side lets you pass with care, but double solid yellow lines forbid passing from either side. [A05]
Why it matters: group center lines; difficulty high; confusable broken versus double solid.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec15-R11 | anchor: A05
Red pavement markers warn of wrong-way travel, while blue markers show the location of fire hydrants or water supplies. [A05]
Why it matters: group pavement markers; difficulty high; confusable red versus blue markers.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0090]
